trails.trailTip: This is a cross-country tundra and creek-bottom route with no trail, signage, or bridges — a topo map, compass or GPS, and river-fording experience are required, and most visitors fly in by air taxi from Bettles or Coldfoot to the Circle Lake or Takahula Lake area first.
trails.didYouKnow: The Arrigetch Peaks' granite spires are sacred to local Iñupiat and Nunamiut people; the name roughly translates to "fingers of the hand outstretched."

trails.trailTip: Follow the same low-elevation pass corridor the Nunamiut have used for generations to cross the Brooks Range — expect tussock tundra, no cell coverage, and to plan your own route since there is no marked path.
trails.didYouKnow: Anaktuvuk Pass is still home to the Nunamiut, the last nomadic Iñupiat caribou-hunting people in North America, and the village sits within the pass itself.

trails.trailTip: Most travelers cover this corridor by packraft or canoe rather than walking it end to end; anyone hiking sections along the gravel bars should still watch for braided channel crossings and sweepers, and carry a satellite communicator since there is no cell service anywhere in the park.
trails.didYouKnow: The Alatna is a federally designated Wild and Scenic River that drains the western Arrigetch Peaks before joining the Koyukuk River.

trails.trailTip: A cross-country tundra walk from the Circle Lake air-taxi drop point; the open tundra makes route-finding easier than in brushy valleys, but sudden weather changes and grizzly encounters are both real considerations at this elevation.
trails.didYouKnow: Circle Lake is a common float-plane access point precisely because its open shoreline offers one of the few reliable landing spots deep in the central Brooks Range.

trails.trailTip: This unmarked route climbs through the park's northern valleys toward the Arctic Divide; carry topo maps and be prepared to reroute around brush and creek fords that a map alone won't show.
trails.didYouKnow: Routes like this one cross the Arctic Divide, the line separating rivers that flow north to the Arctic Ocean from those flowing south to the Yukon.

trails.trailTip: The Noatak corridor is almost always traveled by packraft or canoe rather than on foot end-to-end; anyone hiking gravel bars or side valleys should still carry bear-proof food storage and expect zero resupply options for the entire route.
trails.didYouKnow: The Noatak River drains one of the largest untouched river basins in North America and is a designated Wild and Scenic River for its entire length within the park.

trails.trailTip: Approaching the park's tallest peak means cross-country travel over talus, brush, and potentially glaciated terrain near the summit — this route is for experienced mountaineers with glacier-travel skills, not a casual backcountry hike.
trails.didYouKnow: At 8,276 feet, Mount Igikpak is the highest peak in the central Brooks Range and holds one of the range's few remaining glaciers.

trails.trailTip: Most visitors fly directly onto Walker Lake and day-hike the surrounding tundra ridges from camp rather than walking a set route in; carry a bear-resistant canister since this is an established camping area with routine bear activity.
trails.didYouKnow: Walker Lake sits at the southern boundary of the park and marks the transition from the alpine Brooks Range to the boreal forest of interior Alaska.

animals.whereToLook: River valleys and mountain passes such as Anaktuvuk Pass, along Western Arctic Herd migration corridors
animals.viewingTip: Watch migrating herds from a distance with binoculars or a spotting scope and avoid positioning yourself in a narrow pass or river crossing where your presence could split or redirect the herd.
animals.didYouKnow: The Western Arctic Herd that passes through the park has historically numbered in the hundreds of thousands, one of the largest caribou herds in the world.

animals.whereToLook: Open tundra slopes, river bars, and berry patches throughout the Brooks Range
animals.viewingTip: Keep at least 300 feet (about 100 yards) between yourself and any grizzly, travel in a group while making noise to avoid surprise encounters, carry bear spray, and never approach a berry patch, carcass, or suspected den site a bear is using.
animals.didYouKnow: Brooks Range grizzlies have one of the lowest population densities and slowest reproductive rates of any grizzly population in North America, a consequence of the short arctic growing season.

animals.whereToLook: Steep rocky slopes and cliff bands throughout the Brooks Range
animals.viewingTip: Glass distant slopes with binoculars or a spotting scope rather than climbing toward a band of sheep, especially in late spring and early summer when ewes have young lambs on steep terrain.
animals.didYouKnow: Dall sheep are the only wild, pure-white sheep species in the world and rely on remote cliffs to escape wolves and bears.

animals.whereToLook: Remote river valleys and tundra throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: If you spot a wolf or a den site, observe from far off with binoculars and move away rather than lingering — packs here are among the least human-habituated in North America and disturbance at a den can cause abandonment.
animals.didYouKnow: Gates of the Arctic protects some of the last wolf populations in North America that have never been hunted, trapped, or persecuted by humans in the area they occupy.

animals.whereToLook: Well-drained tundra slopes and esker ridges throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Watch and photograph squirrels from a comfortable distance with a zoom lens rather than approaching a burrow entrance, and never feed them — human food can make wildlife sick and bolder around people.
animals.didYouKnow: Arctic ground squirrels hibernate up to eight months a year and can supercool their body temperature below freezing without freezing solid, the most extreme mammalian hibernation known.

animals.whereToLook: Willow thickets in remote river valleys
animals.viewingTip: Give moose at least 25 yards of space and much more during the fall rut, when bulls can be unpredictable and aggressive — use binoculars rather than closing the distance for a photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Moose in interior Alaska are among the largest in the world, with bulls sometimes exceeding 1,600 pounds.

animals.whereToLook: Open tundra, often trailing larger predators for scraps
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy sightings from a distance and never feed a fox or leave food scraps behind — foxes that lose their fear of people around camps are more likely to be killed by other predators or hit by aircraft, and never approach a den to see pups.
animals.didYouKnow: Arctic fox fur changes from brown-gray in summer to pure white in winter, one of the most complete seasonal camouflage changes of any mammal.

animals.whereToLook: Remote cliffs throughout the Brooks Range
animals.viewingTip: Scan cliff bands with binoculars from below rather than climbing toward a nest ledge, and keep well back from any nest site you spot so incubating or brooding adults aren't flushed off eggs or chicks.
animals.didYouKnow: Golden eagles nesting in the Brooks Range migrate remarkable distances each fall, with some tracked individuals wintering as far south as the Mexican border.
